title: Talk shows and debates: the passive Levantine

blocks.text: Lebanese talk shows are among the most followed in the Arab world, and the Levantine (Lebanese, Syrian, Palestinian, Jordanian) is, after the Egyptian, the dialect that feels most in the media. You don't have to learn to speak: you have to understand it enough to follow a debate, recognize positions and report them. The good news is that you already know the fuṣḥā and the Egyptian: the Levantine is close to both, and with a dozen grammatical words, some pronunciation rules and formulas typical of the debate you can understand much more than you think. In this unity learn the main traits of the Levant (sounds, pronouns, verbs, negation, interrogative words), the lexicon of the debate (breaking, granting, rejecting) and a method to follow a discussion in which everyone speaks together. Three weeks, while the Moroccan track begins (MAG-01).

Targets. At the end of the lesson you know:
1. recognize the Levantine and distinguish it from the Egyptian and the fuṣḥā;
2. understand the main traits: pronunciation, pronouns and suffixes, present with b- and ʿam, future with raḥ, denial, interrogative words;
3. follow a Levant television debate, identifying who claims what and with what arguments and figures;
4. understand the formulas of the debate: interrupt, ask for the floor, grant, reject, thank;
5. report in fuṣḥā, neutrally, a debate heard in Levantine.
